locator: XII.6, 1071b26-29: καίτοι εἰ ὡς λέγουσιν οἱ θεολόγοι οἱ ἐκ νυκτὸς γεννῶντες, ἢ ὡς οἱ φυσικοὶ ὁμοῦ πάντα χρήματά φασι, τὸ αὐτὸ ἀδύνατον. πῶς γὰρ κινηθήσεται, εἰ μὴ ἔσται ἐνεργείᾳ τι αἴτιον;
interpretation: Aristotle reports the theologians who generate all from Night and the physicists who say 'all things were together' as committed to the same thing as the aporia just stated, that potency is prior (1071b23-24, claim ARIST-MET-1071B-POTENCY-PRIOR-A), and objects 'how will it be moved, if there is not some cause in actuality?', which presupposes that on their view things are moved, that is, generated from that origin. Read as: some being is in potency in a respect, no being in act in that respect is simply prior to it, and it is being reduced to act in that respect. Reading steps: (1) 'prior' is simple priority, as in the -A claim on the aporia, not priority in time (DISAMB-PRIORITY-SIMPLE-OR-IN-TIME); on the temporal reading (Night first in time, cf. 1072a7-8: 'chaos or night did not exist for an infinite time') the position is no rival, since Aquinas grants that potency precedes act in time within one changing thing (ST I q.3 a.1 co.). (2) 'generate from Night' is read as the reduction of one such potency to act, motion in the broad sense (DISAMB-MOTION). (3) Weakest reading: one potency in one respect, not every potency, and nothing about the time or duration of the origin. The phrase 'all things together' echoes Anaxagoras, whom Aristotle cites on the other side because his Nous is actuality (1072a4-6); the physicists' view is therefore read as the original mixture taken without an actual moving cause, not as Anaxagoras' whole doctrine. Aristotle rejects the position; the claim records his report of a rival, and Hesiod's and the Orphic texts themselves are not consulted.
